source_document.body:
Every career has a story. In Leadership Lessons , supply chain leaders reflect on the experiences that shaped who they are and how they lead.
What’s Related
Edmund Zagorin’s first business began with a competition he thought he could win. As a college student short on cash, he learned about a business plan contest. Contestants would speak for eight minutes, then answer questions. To someone who had spent years in competitive debate, the format sounded familiar.
Zagorin called a friend with a proposition: “Hey, I think I could win some money. Do you want to start a company with me?” His friend agreed, and the two went on to build a 3D video hardware product and run a film studio in Detroit.
Today, Zagorin is Chief Strategy Officer and co-founder of Arkestro, a predictive procurement company that uses AI to help enterprises make more strategic purchasing decisions. He once expected to make a career of coaching debate teams. Years later, he was taking buses to visit customers to stretch a young company’s savings. Debate was the starting point for much of it.
Finding a place on the debate team
Zagorin was born in France to American parents who met while working as journalists. When he was five, an assignment brought the family to Washington, D.C. He remembers arriving in the United States as a young child and feeling like everyone else already belonged and that he needed to figure out where he fit.
He eventually found that place on his high school debate team. His coach sparked his interest in debate, and having friends on the team helped him stay involved despite poor early results.
“When I started debating, I was probably one of the worst debaters in the country,” he says. He kept going because he loved debating, and by the time he graduated high school, he had won a national championship.
The improvement mattered beyond the trophy. He had found something he wanted to work at, and competition gave him a way to see that work paying off.
He came to understand that the strongest competitors were “the best listeners, not the best talkers.” Listening meant being curious enough to take another person’s perspective seriously, giving their arguments credence, and responding with data , evidence, and research .
He had seen how debate could make people arrogant, but his experience took him in a different direction. “I actually thought that debate helped me find myself,” he says.
Leaving the career he thought he wanted

He later became assistant director of debate at the University of Iowa. Although he enjoyed teaching, he wanted to broaden his horizons, live somewhere different and work in technology . A friend in San Francisco suggested joining a startup.
Zagorin wasn’t sure where he would fit because he wasn’t a software engineer or computer programmer. His friend suggested data science, which he had studied as an undergraduate while researching how social movements use the Internet. In 2015, he moved to San Francisco and joined a startup focused on procurement.
Finding procurement
Procurement was not entirely unfamiliar. At Iowa, Zagorin had taken the university’s procurement training.. He knew about purchasing policies and procedures, but the startup showed him how much data businesses collect and what it can reveal about how they buy.
He later worked in procurement consulting, negotiating purchases that included chemicals and road salt. “I enjoy the work of analyzing spend, figuring out a strategy, and executing it,” he says. He enjoyed the conversations with suppliers that were part of reaching a deal.
Working in procurement gave Zagorin a closer look at how companies spend their money. “Procurement and supply chain are really the largest flows of capital in the world, but they’re not often flowing with great intention,” he says. “That’s partly because the legacy systems and processes were built for compliance and control, rather than value creation and scalable speed.”
He also came to appreciate how little recognition the people making those supply chain decisions received. “I think supply chain people work really hard and don’t always get a lot of credit or appreciation, so I’ve always found common cause with that,” he says.
During the pandemic, more people began to understand his work, including his own family. “ COVID was definitely the first time my mom knew what I did for work,” he says.
“Getting a good price doesn’t matter if the product never shows up.”
People who could afford basic necessities were suddenly unsure whether they could find them. Zagorin knew that uncertainty was already familiar to people who struggled to pay for what they needed. During COVID, having the money wasn’t always enough. “It was a problem that money couldn’t solve,” he says. “Getting a good price doesn’t matter if the product never shows up.”
Building Arkestro
In 2017, Zagorin and his team began developing an AI platform for procurement negotiations, the early work behind Arkestro. The idea came from his experience with sourcing teams, where someone often had a good sense of how a negotiation would end before it began. He wondered whether a machine learning model could use similar information to predict the result.
He started by testing predictions against negotiations he was conducting as a consultant. The team also examined past negotiations, comparing the model’s predictions with the actual results. When they didn’t match, they investigated what the model had missed, such as a personal relationship between a buyer and supplier.
Consulting gave the team a way to earn money while developing the technology. Companies hired them to negotiate purchases, and they used those projects to test what they were building. “That made it a little bit easier to get started just with customers and really build with customers from day one,” he says.
The first two years brought financial uncertainty. Before outside funding, the founders put their savings into the business and cut their spending to give themselves more time. Customer visits sometimes meant sleeping on a friend’s couch. “We took greyhounds instead of flights in some cases,” he says. “We’d stay with friends instead of hotels. For several months we operated from a storage room of an art collective in San Francisco. One of the first predictive negotiations we supported was in an old convent’s chapel because that was where the wifi signal was strongest.”
Looking back, Zagorin is glad he took the chance. He calls it “type two fun,” and those trips have become stories he shares with employees who joined after the early years.
Looking ahead at AI
As Arkestro’s co-founder and Chief Strategy Officer, Zagorin remains confident in its focus on predicting negotiated prices. While much of the attention around AI goes to large language models, he believes Arkestro’s experience with procurement negotiations gives it a head start. Unlike LLMs, Arkestro’s model is focused on predicting the outcome of deals using simulations of multi-party negotiations involving one buyer and one or more suppliers.
“There's a lot of really wise and caring people involved in building these AI companies.”
“Because in a predictive negotiation on Arkestro the buyer makes the first offer to the supplier, our model is somewhat unique because we both predict and influence the deal’s outcome,” says Zagorin. “It’s not like a weather forecast . Our platform is actually creating the offers used in the deal and working through the back-and-forth with multiple suppliers simultaneously. So we predict, but we also make our own weather.”
His outlook for the AI industry is more cautious. He worries that financial pressure around upcoming public offerings could push companies to put commercial interests ahead of responsible decisions about the technology.
At the same time, he sees reasons to be optimistic about the people doing the work. “There's a lot of really wise and caring people involved in building these AI companies,” he says.
He hopes they'll help steer the industry in the right direction, but he expects the next 18 to 24 months to be a wild ride. “I would advise everyone to buckle up.”
